titre: Aspirin, a Name Split in Two by a Judge
accroche: In 1921, a New York judge splits the word “aspirin” in two: a trademark for pharmacists, an everyday word for everyone else.
contenu_vulgarise:
Bayer begins selling acetylsalicylic acid under the name “Aspirin” in the United States in 1899, protected by a patent issued the following year. Until 1904, the company sells only to chemists, doctors and pharmacies, who know Bayer is the maker. From that year on, it sells wholesale, in powder form, to industrial chemists who turn it into tablets themselves and resell it under the single word “Aspirin,” without ever putting Bayer's name on the package: the general public remains unaware of who makes the product until the fall of 1915, when Bayer changes its practice and finally puts its own name on the tablets that reach it. The patent expires in 1917, and in May of that year Bayer Co. sues United Drug Company in a federal court in New York, complaining that it is selling under the name “Aspirin” a product that is not Bayer's. The United States enters the war in 1917, alongside Great Britain and France, and the American government begins seizing German property on its soil, including Bayer's factories, patents and trademarks. On December 12, 1918, the Alien Property Custodian, the federal official in charge of seized foreign property, auctions off Bayer's American business: Sterling Products buys it for $5.31 million.

## What the word means depends on who hears it

Judge Learned Hand rules on April 14, 1921. He poses a single question, he says, in all cases of this kind: “The single question, as I view it, in all these cases, is merely one of fact: What do the buyers understand by the word for whose use the parties are contending?” Hand then distinguishes two audiences. Among pharmacists, doctors and industrial chemists, who buy wholesale and know where the product comes from, the word “Aspirin” has always meant Bayer: the trademark stands. Among the general public, however, anonymous intermediaries sold the product from 1904 to 1915 under that name alone, without ever revealing who made it. The consumer who asks for aspirin has no particular company in mind; he is simply naming a medicine. For him, the word has passed into common language.

Hand therefore grants an injunction that reverses intuition: United Drug remains free to sell to the general public under the single word “aspirin,” with no suffix, but it may no longer use the word in its letters, invoices, labels and other markings for sales to industrial chemists, pharmacists and doctors. To retailers, it may still deliver bottles or boxes of fifty tablets or fewer bearing the word, provided they are placed in an outer package without the word and marked “acetyl salicylic acid manufactured by U.D. Co.” That is where the word continues to mean Bayer, not among the general public.

## One word, two statuses

Hand's test turns on what the buyer understands, not on what the owner registered: Bayer had registered the name as a trademark in May 1899, and that was not enough to keep it among consumers. For them, Judge Hand holds, the name has entered the public domain. The same word can thus carry, at the same moment, two opposite legal statuses depending on the audience that hears it: protected here, fallen into common language there.

carte.punch: A court splits one word in two: a trademark for pharmacists, an ordinary word for everyone else.
carte.idee: In 1921, Judge Learned Hand rules that “Aspirin” remains a trademark among professionals, who know it means Bayer, but has become an ordinary word for the general public, which bought it from 1904 to 1915 without knowing who made it.

quiz.question: On what criterion does Judge Learned Hand distinguish the two statuses of the word “Aspirin” in 1921?
choix: The date on which each category of buyers began obtaining the product on the American market
The price each category of buyers is willing to pay for the medicine at the pharmacy
The buyer's country of origin, the trademark remaining valid outside United States territory alone
What each category of buyers understands by the word: a specific company, or simply a medicine
quiz.explication: Hand poses a question of fact, not of law: what the buyer understands by the word. Professionals, in direct contact with Bayer, continue to see a trademark; the general public, which has only ever known the product's name, sees only a medicine. The same word thus carries two statuses depending on the audience that hears it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why do the American authorities seize Bayer's assets in the United States and then auction them off in 1918?
choix: Because a court finds Bayer guilty of fraud over the Aspirin trademark
Because the United States is at war with Germany and seizes German property on its soil
Because Bayer declares bankruptcy after its patent expires
Because France claims these assets under a wartime treaty
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The United States enters the war in 1917 and seizes German property on its soil, including Bayer's factories, patents and trademarks. On December 12, 1918, Bayer's American business is auctioned off to Sterling Products.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the 1921 injunction, what may United Drug no longer do in its sales to industrial chemists, pharmacists and doctors?
choix: Pay Bayer a royalty on every sale
Use the word “Aspirin” in its letters, invoices and labels
Sell its product to the general public under the single word “aspirin”
Sell them the product, whatever name is used
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The decree reverses intuition: United Drug sells freely to the general public under the single word “aspirin,” but may no longer use that word in its letters, invoices and labels aimed at professionals, precisely where the word continues to mean Bayer. It provides for neither a royalty nor a halt to sales.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Between 1904 and 1915, how does Bayer's product reach the American general public?
choix: It is resold as tablets under the single word Aspirin, without Bayer's name
Bayer sells it directly to consumers as tablets bearing its name
Military hospitals distribute it free to soldiers
European import houses sell it exclusively
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bayer sells wholesale, in powder form, to industrial chemists who make the tablets themselves and resell them without ever putting Bayer's name on them, leaving the public unaware of the origin until 1915.
